newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Analysts predict Ukraine grain disaster.
newsitem.headline: Analysts predict Ukraine grain disaster.

text.p: A government minister in Ukraine, once Europe's breadbasket, on Thursday issued a disastrous forecast for this year's grain crop and analysts said even this could prove optimistic.
Deputy Prime Minister Mykhailo Zubets predicted farmers would bring in 27 million tonnes, a figure which has slipped almost weekly from forecasts of 39 million at the beginning of the harvest season.
Last year's harvest, viewed as mediocre, stood at 36.5 million. In 1990, at the close of the Soviet era, Ukraine brought in a harvest of 51 million tonnes.
"We are counting on getting 27 million tonnes of grain this year," Zubets told Reuters. "Our forecasts for a good harvest were ruined by drought at the beginning of the summer."

Zubets said the nearly-completed grain harvest stood at 21.27 million tonnes. A further two million tonnes were expected from maize (corn) plus four million tonnes from the private farming sector -- twice what it produced last year.
But analysts said even the latest figure might prove optimistic despite forecasts of good autumn harvesting weather.
"It's hard to believe that figure with the further deterioration in the agriculture economy and with the weather as bad as it was," a Western analyst said. "I think it will be 25 million tonnes."
Another Western analyst said 70 days without rain made 25 to 26 million tonnes more realistic. But a trader said the government figure might yet be achieved.
"When all is said and done it could be a tad higher," he said. "Underreporting is common in the interior."

Prior to Soviet rule, Ukraine regularly supplied grain to much of Western Europe. Despite the terrible blow of Stalin's artificial famine which killed millions in the 1930s, it turned in creditable harvests under Communism.
But since independence in 1991, harvest figures have been in virtual freefall.
Farming remains highly collectivised and Soviet-era problems have in fact worsened, including shortages of fuel, equipment, spare parts and storage.

One analyst said that whatever the final figure, this year's harvest would be enough to fill Ukraine's grain needs, which include five to eight million tonnes for human consumption and 15 million tonnes for livestock.
"They will still have export supplies, but the government can't make easy money off it," he said.

Officials said previously that Ukraine expected to export three million tonnes to Russia, the Baltic states and Belarus and would not have to import. Grain sources said Russia may import European and U.S. grain due to its poor harvest.

Zubets said the government was optimistic next year's harvest would bounce back to 40 million tonnes. Plans call for more intensive planting of winter wheat -- traditionally more suited to the country's climate.
"The weather forecast calls for warm conditions at the end of September and a warm October," he said. "We are counting on a much better harvest next year."
